args.text: [lane-marten] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale records: users are sent to old addresses after a server moves, causing outages. (2) Slow recovery: if a bad or poisoned answer is cached, it stays until it expires, so the harm lasts longer. (3) Weak failover: traffic keeps going to a failed server because clients do not see the updated address.

[lane-marten] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate orders or other harmful repeats.

[lane-marten] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Good: ids are roughly time-ordered, so database inserts are friendlier to indexes than random ids, but they are larger (16 bytes) than a plain integer, which uses more storage and memory. (2) They reveal the creation time, which may leak information, and ordering within the same millisecond is not guaranteed.

[lane-marten] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before applying it to the main data, so the change is safely on disk first. After a crash, the database replays the log to restore a consistent state, which keeps committed work from being lost.

[lane-marten] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: a client update can change speed or behaviour, so unpinned runs may differ because of the client rather than the thing being measured. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the same setup later and get comparable results.

[lane-marten] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal that it is full or falling behind, so the senders slow down, wait or are turned away. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make delays worse for everyone.

[lane-marten] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) The same schedule is installed on two servers, for example after scaling out or a copied setup. (2) A slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts. One guard: take a lock before starting, so a second copy sees the lock and exits.

[lane-marten] A tombstone is a marker saying a record was deleted, kept in place of the data itself. In a replicated store it tells other copies to delete the record too, so a copy that missed the delete does not bring the old data back. Tombstones are removed only after a set time, once all copies have seen them.

[lane-marten] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) It passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs. (2) The failure depends on timing, order or environment, for example it fails only when run with other tests, under load, or on one machine.

[lane-marten] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock for a set time, and each machine judges that time by its own clock. With clock skew (machines disagreeing about the time), the holder may think it still has the lock while the lock service thinks it has expired and hands it to someone else. Two holders then act at once, which breaks the lock's promise.

[lane-marten] Two costs of very long feature branches: (1) Merge pain: the longer a branch lives, the further it drifts from the main line, so combining them brings many conflicts and hidden breakage that is hard to untangle. (2) Late feedback: colleagues review a huge change all at once, so problems in design or behaviour are found late, when they are costly to fix.

[lane-marten] A canary release sends a new version to a small share of real users or servers first, while the rest stay on the old version. It checks whether the new version stays healthy under real traffic, such as error rates, speed and resource use, before it is rolled out to everyone.

[lane-marten] Two risks of keeping secrets in environment variables: (1) They leak easily, because crash reports, debug logs, error pages and child processes often print or inherit the whole environment. (2) They are hard to control and rotate, because anyone or anything that can read the process's settings can see them, and changing a secret usually means restarting the service.

[lane-marten] Latency is the time a request takes to get a reply. The p50 (50th percentile, or median) is the time that half of requests beat, so it shows the typical experience. The p99 (99th percentile) is the time that 99 in 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that a small share of users still meet. A service can have a fine p50 and a poor p99.
